# Cubic-tight triangles and an exact circumellipse characterization

Let P_1,P_2,P_3 be the vertices of a nondegenerate planar triangle. Let
nonzero spanning normals v_i satisfy sum v_i=0. Suppose a source y has
strict distinct-vertex incidence: v_i.(P_i-y)>0 and v_i.(P_j-y)<0 for
j!=i. The resulting ordinary row vector is

    f_i=2sqrt(k Q_i)/(sigma_i sum_j Q_j/sigma_j).

Here k is triangle area, Q_i its captured cap area, and sigma_i is the
coarea length of the cutting chord. Write

    L_ij=v_i.(P_i-P_j)>0,        H=sum_i v_i.(P_i-y)>0.

H is independent of y because the normals sum to zero. The exact vertex
cap formula gives f_i^2=4L_ij L_il/H^2. In particular the whole f-vector
is independent of the source as long as strict distinct-vertex incidence
persists. Changing the source translates the signed row margins but leaves
all edge differences and H unchanged.

## 1. Cycle balance is exactly cubic equality

The cube-slab coordinates of
`candidate d61c49578c90db6d` are
u_i=L_i,i+1/H and 1-u_(i+1)=L_i,i+2/H. Its exact deficit identity shows
that

    sum_i f_i^2+f_1f_2f_3=4

if and only if

    L_12 L_23 L_31=L_13 L_32 L_21.                    (1)

Equivalently there are positive mu_i, unique up to a common positive
factor, satisfying detailed balance on every pair:

    mu_i L_ij=mu_j L_ji.                             (2)

Indeed choose mu_1 arbitrarily, determine mu_2 and mu_3 by the pairs
(1,2),(1,3), and use (1) for the remaining pair.

## 2. The associated matrix is positive definite, not merely symmetric

Assume (2). Define the linear map M on two independent edge differences by

    M(P_i-P_j)=mu_i v_i-mu_j v_j.                     (3)

These identities are consistent on the third difference by addition.
They make M symmetric. For example the difference between the two mixed
products on P_1-P_2 and P_1-P_3 is

    mu_1(L_12-L_13)-mu_3(L_32-L_31)
                             +mu_2(L_23-L_21)=0,

by (2).

Put lambda_i=1/mu_i, Lambda=sum lambda_i, and

    O=(sum_i lambda_i P_i)/Lambda.

This point is strictly inside the triangle. Averaging (3) with these
weights and using sum v_i=0 gives

    M(P_i-O)=mu_i v_i.                               (4)

The symmetric quadratic form q(x)=x^T Mx has the same value R on all
x_i=P_i-O, since

    q(x_i)-q(x_j)
      =(P_i-P_j).(mu_i v_i+mu_j v_j)
      =mu_i L_ij-mu_j L_ji=0.

Also every edge has positive squared value

    q(P_i-P_j)=2mu_i L_ij>0.                         (5)

The weighted variance identity, valid for every symmetric form, yields

    Lambda^2 R=sum_(i<j) lambda_i lambda_j
                                      q(P_i-P_j)>0.  (6)

Thus R>0. Let G_ij=x_i^T Mx_j. From (5),
G_ij=R-mu_i L_ij<R. The positive dependence sum lambda_i x_i=0 implies

    G_ij/R=(lambda_l^2-lambda_i^2-lambda_j^2)
                                      /(2lambda_i lambda_j).

The strict upper bound G_ij<R therefore proves all three strict triangle
inequalities lambda_l<lambda_i+lambda_j. Their other two versions imply
lambda_l>|lambda_i-lambda_j, and hence G_ij>-R as well. Consequently
the two-by-two Gram matrix on any x_i,x_j has positive diagonal R and
positive determinant R^2-G_ij^2. These two vectors are independent because
O is strictly inside the triangle. Therefore M is positive definite on
the plane.

## 3. Exact geometric equivalence

The set

    E={x:(x-O)^T M(x-O)<=R}

is an actual ellipse passing through all three triangle vertices. Its
outward normal at P_i is a positive multiple of M(P_i-O)=mu_i v_i.
Thus a cubic-tight triangle has a circumellipse whose normals at its
vertices agree with the three cap normals. The ellipse center is strictly
inside the triangle, and both its center and its quadratic form up to scale
are determined by the edge data.

Conversely suppose an ellipse with positive definite form M passes through
P_i and its outward normal there is a positive multiple mu_i v_i. Equality
of the three quadratic values gives (2), hence (1) and cubic equality.

This proves an exact equivalence for strict distinct-vertex triangles.
After the common invertible transformation M^(1/2), it says that the
triangle is inscribed in a circle with interior circumcenter and the
three normal directions point radially outward at its vertices. All
halfspaces and coarea factors must be transformed together; no assertion
about a mixed-integer lattice is made.

The characterization does not show that adding an ear to this triangle
preserves the cubic, either locally or at finite size. It identifies the
complete equality geometry on which such a first-variation claim would
have to be proved, including asymmetric equality vectors whose separate
Lorentz rows are all strict.

## 4. Complete equality incidence for arbitrary triangle cuts

The now-proved stochastic theorem in
`candidate 6b3596acb8604c8b` gives the
cubic for ALL interior-source triangle cuts. Its equality argument also
determines the incidence: if any cap contains two strict triangle vertices,
the cubic inequality is strict.

Here is the full equality proof. The actual transfer constructs a
nonnegative column-stochastic matrix X whose row entries are positive
multiples of captured edge-length fractions, and f_i=2phi(X_i)>0. If the
cubic is an equality, the three-cycle matrix has spectral radius one and
a strictly positive unit Perron eigenvector. Holding that eigenvector
fixed shows that X maximizes a strictly positive weighted sum of its three
row phi values over ALL column-stochastic matrices. Section 2 of the
stochastic theorem therefore permits at most one fully positive row.

A cap with two strict captured vertices has a positive captured fraction
on every triangle edge, so its row is fully positive. The other two rows
must then each have a zero. Because their phi values are positive, neither
can have two zeros: for a row with only one nonzero entry, phi=0. Thus
each has exactly one zero and its other two entries are positive.

Apply the two-zero-row boundary proof. If the chosen zeros are in the same
column, the remaining full row has the form (1,c,r) with 0<c,r<1, because
both of the other rows are positive in those latter columns. Hence
F_full=c+r-cr<1, and

    aq+bp >=2sqrt(abpq)>2sqrt(abpq F_full)

is strict. This excludes cubic equality.

If the zeros are in different columns, write the matrix in the proof's
form [0,a,b; c,0,e; r,s,t]. Full positivity and the two positive entries
in each other row imply r,s,t in (0,1). Every displayed difference between
Z and a candidate row-three quadratic is then strictly positive. Therefore
z=F_full<Z<1. The matrix N=(1-z)I-(1-t)M has strictly positive
determinant (1-z)(Z-z) and nonnegative diagonal, hence is positive
definite. Its quadratic-form estimate on (sqrt(b),sqrt(e)) is strict,
again excluding equality.

Consequently no cap can contain two strict vertices at equality. Each
vertex is strictly captured by at least one cap: its three signed margins
sum to zero, cannot all vanish because the normals span and the source is
interior, and therefore include a positive one. Three caps, each capturing
at most one strict vertex, must thus match the three vertices bijectively.
After relabeling, the diagonal margins are positive and every off-diagonal
margin is nonpositive. Off-diagonal zeros, corresponding to a cutting line
through a different vertex, are retained.

In this weak distinct-vertex incidence the exact vertex-cap and cubic
deficit formulas follow directly from their intercept expressions, or by
perturbing the signed vertex data toward strict incidences and taking limits.
All edge drops L_ij remain strictly positive because the own-vertex margin
is positive. Thus the detailed-balance proof and the positive-definite
circumellipse construction in Sections 1--3 apply unchanged.

It follows that every equality case of the arbitrary-incidence triangle
cubic has weak distinct-vertex incidence and the circumellipse normal
geometry proved above. Conversely this geometry together with weak
distinct-vertex incidence gives equality. A cap containing two strict
vertices always gives a strict inequality.
